title: Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) signs MoU with TRIFED to Strengthen Market Access for PM Vishwakarma Artisans
subtitle:
TRIFED to facilitate onboarding, capacity building, product promotion and market access through Tribes India retail outlets and its online marketplace

Collaboration to establish a “Tribes India–PM Vishwakarma Collection” and expand the visibility of products made by artisans
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                05 NOV 2026 8:34PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises, signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the Tribal Cooperative Marketing Development Federation of India (TRIFED), under the Ministry of Tribal Affairs, to strengthen market access for eligible tribal artisans registered under the PM Vishwakarma Scheme. The MoU was signed in the presence of Dr. Rajneesh, Additional Secretary & Development Commissioner, Ministry of MSME; Shri M. Raja Murugan, Managing Director, TRIFED; along with Shri Nitish Kumar, Deputy Director General (DDG); Shri Danish Ashraf, Joint Development Commissioner, Ministry of MSME;  and Shri Prateek Singh Meena, Executive Director, TRIFED.
The collaboration brings together the Ministry of MSME’s PM Vishwakarma framework and TRIFED’s established Tribes India marketplace and retail network.
The PM Vishwakarma Scheme, launched on 17 September 2023, seeks to improve the quality and reach of the products and services of traditional artisans and craftspeople. The Scheme supports artisans whose         skills are passed from generation to generation through the traditional guru-shishya model of training within families and informal groups.
Objectives of the MoU
:-
Under the MoU, the Ministry of MSME and TRIFED will collaborate to facilitate the display, promotion and sale of products made by eligible tribal artisans registered under PM Vishwakarma scheme. The collaboration will cover product-based trades such as carpenter, metalsmith, sculptor, goldsmith, potter, shoe smith, basket, mat /broom maker/ coir weaver, doll and toy maker, garland maker, etc.
TRIFED will facilitate the onboarding and capacity building of eligible tribal artisans referred by the Ministry of MSME and provide them market access through the Tribes India retail network and its online marketplace, subject to applicable onboarding conditions and policies.
Products made by participating tribal artisans will be displayed through the Tribes India retail network and on tribesindia.com under the proposed “Tribes India–PM Vishwakarma Collection”, subject to sellers’ consent and compliance with applicable TRIFED policies.
TRIFED will facilitate aggregation, quality assurance and packaging support for market-ready products and will work with the Ministry of MSME to provide initial product imaging and cataloguing support to mutually identified sellers.
TRIFED will facilitate promotion of products made by identified tribal Vishwakarmas through its e-marketplace and provide dedicated display and sales space across its outlets, subject to the provisions and applicable terms of the MoU.
The Ministry of MSME will identify and facilitate potential sellers, encourage them to list products across different categories on tribesindia.com, conduct awareness workshops and support coordination between artisans and TRIFED.
TRIFED’s product portfolio includes tribal textiles, metal crafts, cane and bamboo products, organic foods, tribal paintings, jewellery and pottery, while its retail outlets showcase tribal handloom and handicraft products from communities across the country.
This collaboration represents an important step towards expanding the market visibility of tribal artisans registered under PM Vishwakarma by connecting their traditional products with the Tribes India retail and digital marketplace network. It will support product presentation, capacity building and broader market access for participating artisans, in accordance with the applicable terms and policies of the two organisations.

title: Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) organised an awareness workshop on SRI Fund for supporting Women-Led MSMEs
subtitle:
Ministry of MSME highlights the role of SRI Fund in mobilising Growth Capital for Women-Led Enterprises under Yashashvini Campaign

SRI Fund leverages nearly ₹48,000 Crore in Private Investment, supports 824 MSMEs
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                05 NOV 2026 1:37PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME), Government of India, organised an “Awareness Workshop on the Self-Reliant India (SRI) Fund for Supporting Women-Led MSMEs” on 4 November 2026 at Kartavya Bhawan 3, New Delhi, as part of the Yashashvini Campaign for promoting women entrepreneurship. The event was chaired by Shri Bharat Khera, Secretary (MSME).
The workshop brought together over 60 women entrepreneurs from across the country, along with senior officials from the Ministry of MSME, representatives of industry associations, NSIC Venture Capital Fund Limited (NVCFL). SBI Ventures Limited (SVL), Daughter Funds under the SRI Fund, Women Entrepreneurship Platform (WEP) of NITI Aayog and Atal Incubation Centre ALEAP Women Entrepreneurs Hub.
Dr. Rajneesh, Additional Secretary & Development Commissioner, Ministry of MSME, gave an overview of the journey of the SRI Fund. He explained that the Fund was conceived to extend equity support to MSMEs beyond traditional debt, with a ₹10,000 crore commitment from the Government of India, and an expectation that private investors would contribute four times that amount. He noted that, in several cases, investee enterprises associated with the SRI Fund had grown their turnover three to four times within two to three years, and had gone on to raise further capital from private sources. He urged the associations present to carry the message about the Fund to their members.
In his inaugural address, Shri Bharat Khera said that registrations on the Udyam and Udyam Assist portals had crossed 10 crore on 30 October 2026, which had bridged the formalisation gap. Of these, 37.6 per cent were women-owned enterprises, and now, let us aspire to take this share to 50 per cent. He noted that formalisation now placed a greater responsibility on the Ministry to help MSMEs scale up – for which, growth capital is critical.
Shri Khera shared that, under the SRI Fund, commitments of ₹8,305 crore had been made against the ₹10,000 crore corpus, and that nearly ₹48,000 crore had been leveraged from private venture capital and private equity funds. 72 Daughter Funds have been empanelled, and investments of ₹21,330 crore have already been made in 824 MSMEs, of which about 74 per cent are micro enterprises. Of the enterprises supported, 77 have moved up to a larger category, six have been listed on stock exchanges, and 32 exits have been completed with profits. He added that Daughter Funds take investment decisions on commercial lines, looking at viability, growth trajectory over the last three years, and a business plan with positive cash flows. The Government maintains an arm’s length from their day-to-day operations and does not play any role in Daughter Funds’ investment decisions.
Secretary also stressed that credit and equity must go together. He said that MSME credit outstanding had grown from about ₹10 lakh crore in 2014 to over ₹40 lakh crore, with the non-performing assets for MSME sector falling to about 3.5 per cent. He highlighted that an additional ₹2,000 crore has been provided to the SRI Fund in Union Budget 2026-27, for micro enterprises. He also drew attention to the newly rolled out ₹10,000 crore SME Growth Fund, which will invest directly in small and medium enterprises. He advised entrepreneurs to maintain proper financial records and adopt a suitable legal structure, and said that bringing in equity also improves an enterprise’s access to debt.
In Session I, titled ‘The growth journey of women-led MSMEs – why growth capital matters’, representatives of industry associations shared their experience of working with women entrepreneurs. They pointed out that many women-led enterprises that are early-stage require support through smaller tickets, investment-readiness programmes in Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities, support in accounting and business valuation, and flexibility for women entrepreneurs who may lack collateral or long balance-sheet histories. They also stressed the need to link capital with market access, including through the Government e-Marketplace (GeM), ONDC and exports, and emphasized the importance of organizing such workshops regularly.
In Session II, on the ‘Overview of the SRI Fund and the role of Daughter Funds’, Shri Praveen Kumar, Additional Development Commissioner, Ministry of MSME, explained the structure of the Fund, in which the Mother Fund invests only through Daughter Funds, and the Daughter Funds invest in MSMEs. Shri Subhransu Sekhar Acharya, Chairman-cum-Managing Director, NSIC, spoke on the gaps in the MSME ecosystem and advised entrepreneurs on the benefits of equity funding. Shri Prem Prabhakar, MD and CEO of SBI Ventures Limited, the investment manager of the SRI Fund, said that equity is of strategic value for growing enterprises as it does not require collateral and because investors provide sector specific mentorship and hand-holding. The Daughter Funds explained the investment criteria such as a strong market, a capable team, a scalable model, audited financials, governance readiness, including a private limited company structure, and a clear use of capital. They advised entrepreneurs on the common steps for acquiring equity funding, from screening to due diligence and documentation.
In Session III, the focus was on support available through ecosystem partners. Representatives from the Atal Incubation Centre ALEAP Women Entrepreneurs Hub and the Women Entrepreneurship Platform (WEP), NITI Aayog, presented the range of support available to women entrepreneurs, including incubation, mentorship, market access, access to information on government schemes, and compliance support. Technical support for the conceptualisation, planning, and execution of the workshop was provided by the ecosystem partner MicroSave Consulting (MSC).
The final session was an interactive Q&A where participants broached subjects such as approaching Daughter Funds, investment-readiness for proprietorship-run enterprises, sector-specific funds, and technology and infrastructure support. It was shared that details of the 72 Daughter Funds, including their sector focus and contacts, are available on the website of NSIC Venture Capital Fund Limited, the special purpose vehicle for the SRI Fund.  The workshop concluded with the Ministry of MSME assuring continued support to women entrepreneurship through the Yashashvni Campaign in the future.

title: Day 1 of 4th Conference of Mining Ministers Witnesses Major Initiatives, Key Deliberations and Renewed Push for Centre–State Coordination
date:

                05 NOV 2026 9:29PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The first day of the two-day 4th Conference of Mining Ministers, organised by the Ministry of Mines in Goa, witnessed the participation of Chief Minister of Goa, Dr. Pramod Sawant; Union Minister of Coal and Mines, Shri G. Kishan Reddy; Minister of State for Coal and Mines, Shri Satish Chandra Dubey; Secretary, Ministry of Mines, Shri Keshav Chandra; Secretary, Ministry of Coal; Mining Ministers from various States; and senior officials from the Ministries of Mines and Coal.
The day witnessed the launch of three significant initiatives aimed at strengthening mineral exploration, enhancing transparency and promoting technology-driven mineral governance. The 9th Tranche of Critical and Strategic Mineral Block Auction was launched, offering 20 mineral blocks across 8 States, including strategically important minerals such as Rare Earth Elements, Graphite and Vanadium. This was followed by the launch of the 3rd Tranche of Exploration Licence Auction, comprising 11 exploration blocks across 6 States, unlocking the country’s untapped mineral potential.
The dignitaries also launched ANVESH and EKAM, two digital portals developed by the Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM), to strengthen data-driven governance and informed decision-making. ANVESH (Analytics and Navigation for Valuation, Evaluation and Strategic Headway in Mining) will facilitate access to and analysis of important mining-related data, including mineral production, despatch, sale quantities, average sale prices and imports and exports. These initiatives mark important steps towards strengthening India’s mineral security and modernising the mining ecosystem.
Addressing the conference, Minister of State for Coal and Mines, Shri Satish Chandra Dubey, highlighted the importance of effective coordination between the Centre and States, strengthening exploration activities and addressing challenges in the mining sector.
Chief Minister of Goa, Dr. Pramod Sawant, highlighted the importance of the mining sector in Goa’s economic development and emphasised sustainable mining practices, responsible resource utilisation and cooperation between the Centre and States.
Union Minister of Coal and Mines, Shri G. Kishan Reddy, underscored the strategic importance of the mining and coal sectors in achieving the vision of Viksit Bharat @2047. He emphasised strengthening domestic mineral production, accelerating exploration, promoting processing, refining and recycling of critical minerals, adopting modern technologies and enhancing Centre–State cooperation.
Secretary, Ministry of Mines, Shri Keshav Chandra, highlighted the importance of active participation by States and close coordination with the Central Government for the effective development of the mining sector. He emphasised the need to address challenges, accelerate mineral exploration and unlock the country’s mineral potential.
Secretary, Ministry of Coal, highlighted key priorities of coal sector and the importance of coordinated efforts between the Centre and States in strengthening the coal sector and addressing emerging challenges.
The Additional Secretary, Ministry of Mines, made a detailed presentation on key developments, initiatives and priorities in the mining sector, covering mineral exploration, auction of mineral blocks, critical and strategic minerals, domestic mineral production and issues requiring coordinated action by the Centre and States. The Additional Secretary, Ministry of Coal, also made a detailed presentation on key issues, sectoral challenges and priority initiatives for strengthening the coal sector.
Mining Ministers from participating States shared detailed perspectives on the challenges, issues and priorities concerning the mining sector in their respective States. They highlighted State-specific concerns, implementation-related challenges and areas requiring the attention and support of the Central Government. The discussions provided an important platform for States to present their views, share experiences and deliberate on measures to address bottlenecks and accelerate the development of the mining sector.
The first day concluded with constructive deliberations and a renewed emphasis on strengthening Centre–State coordination, addressing the concerns of States and advancing the development of India’s mining and coal sectors. The conference will continue on 6 November 2026 with further discussions on key priorities and the way forward.

Third Tranche of Exploration Licence (EL) Auction Also Launched

title: BRE Summit & Expo 2026 Reinforces India’s Position as a Major Global Force in Renewable Energy: Union New & Renewable Energy Minister Shri Pralhad Joshi
subtitle: The Summit reinforces India's position as a resilient clean-energy economy, an attractive investment destination and a global partner for sustainable development: Shri Joshi
ministry: Ministry of New and Renewable Energy
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                05 NOV 2026 5:19PM by PIB Delhi
content:
India has emerged as a major global force in renewable energy, with the world taking notice of its progress and growing ambitions, said Union Minister for New and Renewable Energy, Education and Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution, Shri Pralhad Joshi, while addressing the media at the conclusion of the Bharat Renewable Energy (BRE) Summit 2026 here today.
He said that Bharat Mandapam had brought together global policymakers, investors, industry leaders and innovators from across the world. With participation from more than 135 countries, the Summit emerged as one of India's largest global platforms for renewable energy. He noted that this was the first time that three important events in the renewable energy sector had been held together, with overwhelming participation from domestic and international stakeholders demonstrating global confidence in India's renewable energy growth story.
The Summit was inaugurated by the Hon’ble Prime Minister on 2nd November 2026. In his address, the Prime Minister highlighted the strategic importance of India's sustained investments in renewable energy in strengthening the country's resilience to global disruptions, arising from COVID-19 pandemic and the West Asia crisis. He observed that India’s investment in the renewable energy sector has largely shielded the country from these disruptions.
The Prime Minister underscored that India's renewable energy journey is not only transforming its domestic energy landscape but also generating solutions and experiences that can benefit the world. Emphasising India's commitment to sharing its innovations and achievements with humanity, he highlighted the potential of India's clean energy success to support the energy transition in countries across the world. Calling for greater participation in the clean energy innovation ecosystem, the Prime Minister invited startups, IITs, innovators and entrepreneurs to develop solutions and business models through which an increasing number of household energy requirements can be met using clean energy.
Organised from 2nd-5th November, the four-day summit brought together global policymakers, industry leaders, investors, technology providers, researchers, startups and international institutions on a common platform to advance the clean energy transition. The Summit witnessed strong participation with over 75000 visitors, 400 plus exhibitors and more than 627 speakers across 113 sessions, with representation from 135 countries with about 800 delegates, including the Partner countries, ISA members, International Organisations, and Diplomatic Missions located in India. High-level ministerial participation included 32 international Ministers, 6 Chief Ministers and 10 State Energy Ministers, reflecting strong engagement from both national and sub-national stakeholders.
By bringing together policymakers, investors, industry, research institutions, startups and international development partners, the Summit has strengthened confidence in India's clean energy market and helped translate national and global ambitions into a forward-looking agenda for implementation.
The summit highlighted that India's clean energy policies and democratisation of the energy transition, decoupling economic development from fossil-fuel emissions. India has accelerated its energy transition in the last few years, with more than a quarter of India's annual electricity consumption coming from renewable energy sources in the last financial year. India's experience proved that sustained investments in renewable energy, supported by enabling and stable policy regime, institutional reforms and technology innovations, can strengthen energy security while supporting economic growth.
A major outcome of the Summit was the strong confidence expressed by domestic and international investors in India's clean energy investment opportunity. To achieve the national target of 500 GW of non-fossil fuel capacity, India requires investments of approximately USD 220 billion. Discussions during the Summit showed that the availability of capital is not a constraint, with investors expressing positive interest in India's long-term clean energy growth prospects, extending well beyond the immediate 2030 requirements.
Importantly, investor participation extended beyond traditional strategic investors to include pension funds, institutional investors, and providers of long-term patient capital, reflecting the growing depth of India's clean energy financing ecosystem.
The deliberations highlighted the importance of bankable power purchase agreements, predictable offtake arrangements, clearer risk allocation and deeper bond markets. The role of new instruments like Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs) and blended finance in mobilising capital at scale was also discussed.
The Union Minister of New & Renewable Energy held several high-level engagements during the Summit, including a CEO level clean energy Investment Roundtable wherein the Chief Ministers, State Energy Ministers, Senior Government officials and Industry leaders participated. The round table identified priorities for turning renewable energy ambition into delivery. These include synchronised planning of generation, transmission, storage and demand centres, and greater certainty in land, approvals and execution. Besides this, he held bilateral meetings with the French Minister Delegate of Ecological Transition and Denmark's Minister for Business and Competitiveness. The leaders discussed the issues of common interest and that of global energy scenarios. The Summit also provided platform to more than 100 Business-to-Business (B2B) meetings that were held on the sidelines which provided businesses with opportunities for partnerships and collaboration.
The Summit's deliberations reflected the evolution of India's clean energy agenda from expanding installed renewable energy capacity towards building a reliable, flexible and integrated power system. With rising electricity demand from industry, cooling, electric mobility and data centres, the next phase of the transition will require greater emphasis on energy storage, transmission infrastructure, grid flexibility, ancillary services, forecasting, demand response and green open access.
Energy storage emerged as one of the most important near-term priorities. Discussions also emphasised the need to align storage and transmission planning with renewable energy procurement and emerging demand centres, while strengthening institutions, grid management, and modern AI-based systems to forecast wind and solar generation. New contracts and technical designs like Round-the-clock Renewable Energy and Firm and Dispatchable Renewable Energy (FDRE), including the globally competitive rate of Rs. 5.25/ unit discovered in the recent SECI tender, were also discussed. It attracted a huge interest from the foreign delegates and policymakers.
The Summit also highlighted the growing importance of green procurement in enhancing industrial competitiveness, supporting exports and accelerating industrial decarbonisation. It also highlighted the growing interest in the transition from petro-economy, dependent on fossil fuels, to electro-economy, based on independent electrical power systems.
Deepening India's domestic clean energy manufacturing ecosystem was another major focus of BRE Summit & Expo 2026. Discussions emphasised the need to move beyond assembly towards domestic manufacturing of materials, components, equipment and advanced technologies, supported by shared laboratories, pilot manufacturing lines, demonstration facilities and testing and certification infrastructure.
The Summit brought together stakeholders working across next-generation solar technologies, perovskite cells, recyclable wind turbine materials, long-duration energy storage, electrolysers, fuel cells, artificial intelligence use cases in renewable energy and floating solar.
The Summit placed particular emphasis on connecting research and innovation with commercial deployment. Public procurement, field demonstrations, testing and certification infrastructure and collaboration between industry and research institutions were identified as important instruments for accelerating the commercialisation of Indian technologies.
Youth participation and entrepreneurship were integral to the innovation agenda. The Summit saw strong participation of more than 300 startups across growth and early stage in the RE Hackathon. Strong participation across youth from IIT/Universities/Colleges/schools was also seen in the RE GEN Challenge. The innovation ecosystem in the expo featured 70 startup pods, 40 academic posters and 10 research papers, bringing together young talent, researchers, and entrepreneurs to contribute to India's emerging clean energy technology ecosystem.
The Fourth International Conference on Green Hydrogen provided an important platform for advancing India's green hydrogen ambitions, with discussions focusing on the development of dependable domestic demand, long-term offtake arrangements, export opportunities, standards & certification, testing and safety frameworks.
An important commercial development was the signing of an MoU between Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI) and Power2X, from Rotterdam to advance the supply and offtake of green molecules from India to international markets. The first tranche indicated a potential volume of 3 lakh tonnes per annum of green methanol, reflecting the growing opportunities for India in emerging global green molecule markets.
The Ninth Session of the ISA Assembly marked an important milestone in international solar cooperation. The Assembly considered the Director General's Report for 2026, the Workplan and Budget for 2027, audited accounts for 2025 and proposals relating to Partner Organisation status for the African Union, COMESA, SELCO, SNV and the All India Discoms Association.
A major international announcement was the proposed USD 200 million Africa Solar Facility under the ISA, aimed at facilitating greater access to finance and accelerating solar deployment across African countries. Discussions identified project aggregation, blended finance, patient capital, local-currency financing and payment-risk mitigation as important instruments for mobilising investment. The Africa50 Distributed Renewable Energy Fund and Nigeria DRE Fund were highlighted as financing models. The Africa50 DRE Fund is designed to address investment barriers associated with smaller DRE projects, including project-level and payment risks, through a combination of regional and global financing structures. The Francophone and Sahel Energy Resilience Initiative was also highlighted, focusing on solar-plus-storage solutions for critical power requirements, rooftop solar for public facilities and productive-use solar for agriculture and livelihoods.
Drawing upon India's experience in solarising agricultural pumps, the ISA also advanced its ambition of deploying one million solar pumps globally. The ISA Small Island Developing States (SIDS) Platform aims to facilitate up to 500 MW of solar capacity across SIDS by 2030. The SUNRISE photovoltaic and battery circularity network has expanded to 35 countries.
These initiatives reflect India's approach of combining domestic experience, technology, financing, capacity building and implementation capabilities to support the clean energy aspirations of the Global South.
The Summit saw the launch of the ISA Academy and the Global Capability Centre – SHINE, aimed at strengthening capacity building, digital learning, and cooperation in grid-related areas. A total of 10 MoUs and Framework Agreements were signed during the Summit, expanding cooperation across technology, research, capacity building, manufacturing and project implementation.
Framework Agreements were signed by ISA with Breakthrough Energy Ventures, the India Energy & Climate Center at the University of California, Berkeley, and Schneider Electric Foundation. MoUs were signed by ISA with Shakti Pumps (India) Limited and Railway Energy Management Company Limited, among other partnerships announced during the Summit.
The BRE Summit & Expo 2026 also strengthened the knowledge and evidence base of India's renewable energy ecosystem through the release of 37 reports, assessments, guidebooks and digital platforms.
The publications released at the event cover policy, manufacturing, deployment, skilling and safety, and should strengthen the renewable energy ecosystem on each of these fronts.
Ease of Doing Solar
and the Renewable Energy State Assessment Framework (RE-SAF) give policymakers and states a common basis for benchmarking progress and identifying barriers. The National Hydrogen Survey adds to this for the green hydrogen sector. The studies on solar manufacturing, wind indigenisation and battery electrolyte show where domestic capacity gaps remain and where industry can build supply chains. The Skilling Blueprint for the top 100 RE districts links workforce readiness to deployment. Taken together, these publications should give investors, developers, utilities and state agencies clearer evidence to plan and decide on. They should also improve coordination between government, industry and development partners, and support India’s push for domestic manufacturing and faster deployment.
The Summit reaffirmed India's commitment to achieving its clean energy goals while contributing to global energy security, sustainable development and climate action. It also demonstrated that India's renewable energy journey is increasingly defined not only by the scale of capacity addition, but by its ability to develop integrated energy systems, attract long-term investment, foster innovation, strengthen domestic manufacturing and share successful solutions with the world.

India’s remarkable progress in renewable energy demonstrates that environmental commitments are not a hindrance to economic growth but a catalyst for the country’s development journey, said the Vice-President of India, Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan, while addressing the Valedictory Session of the Bharat Renewable Energy Summit & Expo 2026 here today.
The Vice-President highlighted India’s achievements in the renewable energy sector, its commitment to sustainable development and the transformative role of clean energy in empowering households, farmers and communities across the country.
The Vice-President said that the progress achieved over the last decade vindicates Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi’s vision that environmental commitments are catalysts for growth, delivering greater energy access, lower industrial costs, employment opportunities and reduced import dependence. Calling for stronger industry-academia collaboration, he said, “The technologies of 2040 will come from the laboratories and start-ups of today,” emphasising the importance of research, innovation and entrepreneurship.
Union Minister for New and Renewable Energy, Education and Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution, Shri Pralhad Joshi, said that India’s Renewable Energy sector has attracted more than ₹15 lakh crore in investment over the past decade, while addressing the ceremony. He said that nearly ₹6 lakh crore had flowed into the sector in just the last two years.
Shri Joshi stated that BRE Summit & Expo 2026 is the largest renewable energy event hosted in India, with over 75,000 visitors from 135 countries, participation from more than 32 international Ministers, over eight partner countries and the European Union. The Summit also brought together 14 States and Union Territories as partners, six Chief Ministers, 10 State Energy Ministers, over 400 exhibitors, more than 620 speakers and 113 sessions. It also featured the 9th International Solar Alliance Assembly and the 4th International Conference on Green Hydrogen.
The Union Minister stated that four days ago, participants had come together with a shared ambition to shape the next phase of the global energy transition. As the Summit concluded, he expressed pride in the achievements and stated that India had taken its renewable energy story to the world. He said that the Watts Next forum brought innovators together, while the Next Terawatt Ministerial Plenary addressed integrated energy planning, resilient infrastructure, storage and financing.
Shri Joshi further highlighted a major decision taken the previous day, under which the Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, approved a ₹14,500 crore Viability Gap Funding (VGF) scheme for the development of 92 GWh of grid-scale energy storage capacity. This includes 30 GWh of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), 60 GWh of Pumped Storage Projects (PSPs) and 2 GWh through new technologies.
Shri Joshi also stated that India had achieved utility-scale solar generation costs of USD 30–35 per MWh (₹2,840–₹3,313), the lowest in the world. Renewable energy had helped India save more than USD 100 billion in fossil fuel imports, equivalent to approximately ₹9.46 lakh crore.
He further highlighted that in 2025, India auctioned 15 GW of hybrid renewable energy projects, taking the total auctioned capacity to 64 GW, with both figures representing the highest volumes anywhere in the world. The average tariffs achieved between 2023 and 2025 stood at around USD 45 per MWh (₹4,260), which was 20 per cent below the average cost of electricity from coal-fired power plants.
Highlighting India's growing manufacturing capabilities, the Minister stated that solar module manufacturing capacity had crossed 225 GW, making India the world's second-largest manufacturer of solar modules. He further stated that distributed solar capacity for self-consumption would exceed 100 GW by 2030.
The Union Minister noted that these figures had also been featured in the International Energy Agency's (IEA) report,
India RE Market Report 2026: Analysis and Forecast to 2030
, which was launched during the Summit.
During the Summit, Shri Joshi held bilateral discussions with France, Denmark, the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and several countries from the Global South to explore opportunities for cooperation and investment.
The Summit witnessed the participation of 800 international delegates from different countries and the signing of 10 MoUs and framework agreements, including the SECI MoU, which has the potential for the supply of 3 lakh tonnes of green methanol per annum.
Emphasising the importance of strengthening energy infrastructure alongside renewable energy expansion, Shri Joshi stated that the growing renewable energy capacity would require stronger transmission networks, greater storage capacity and smarter grids. He highlighted that digitalisation and Artificial Intelligence would become very important in forecasting, predictive maintenance and energy management.
The Minister further stated that AI data centres were expected to add 26.3 GW of electricity demand by 2031-32. He emphasised the need to plan for this additional load, with renewable energy playing the primary role in meeting the demand. He stated, “AI will power the future. Clean energy will power AI.”
Concluding his address, Shri Joshi reiterated that Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi had given India a target at BRESE 2026. He expressed confidence that the industry had the capacity, investors had the confidence, and international partners were ready to work together towards achieving the target.
Minister of State for New and Renewable Energy and Power, Shri Shripad Yesso Naik; Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India, Dr. Ajay Kumar Sood; and Secretary, Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, Shri Santosh Kumar Sarangi, were present on the occasion. Representatives of partner countries, policymakers, investors, industry leaders, knowledge partners, exhibitors and other delegates also participated in the Summit.

title: NRAA, ICAR-NBSS&LUP and DoLR Organise National-Level Consultation to Strengthen Science-Based Watershed Management
subtitle:
Shri. Dilip Kumar, Secretary, DoLR calls for balancing scientific rigour with practical implementation, flexibility and community participation

National Technical Guidelines to provide a scientific and practical framework for future watershed development programmes
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                05 NOV 2026 12:19PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Department of Land Resources (DoLR), Ministry of Rural Development, The National Rainfed Area Authority (NRAA), Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, in collaboration with the ICAR–National Bureau of Soil Survey and Land Use Planning (ICAR-NBSS&LUP), Nagpur, has organised a two-day , 3rd National Level Consultation Meeting on the Draft National Technical Guidelines (NTG) for Improved Watershed Management under World Bank Assisted “Rejuvenating Watersheds for Agricultural Resilience through Innovative Development (REWARD)” Programme on November 4–5, 2026, at ICAR-NBSS&LUP, Nagpur. The consultation brings together senior policymakers, technical experts, development partners, researchers and representatives of various States to deliberate on strengthening watershed development through scientific, technology-driven, cost-effective and participatory approaches.
The inaugural session was attended by Shri Dilip Kumar, IAS, Secretary, Department of Land Resources, Dr. Chandra Sekhar Kumar, IAS, CEO, National Rainfed Area Authority (NRAA), Shri Nitin Khade, IAS, Joint Secretary, Department of Land Resources, Ms. Priti Kumar, Senior Agriculture Specialist and Task Team Leader, World Bank, Dr. Susama Sudhishri, Technical Expert (Watershed Development) NRAA and Dr. N.G. Patil, Director, ICAR-NBSS&LUP, along with other distinguished delegates.
Addressing the inaugural session, Secretary, DoLR, Shri Dilip Kumar emphasised the need to strike a balance between scientific rigour and practical implementation in watershed development programmes. He observed that technical guidelines should not become so rigid that they create difficulties for field-level implementation. Flexibility must be provided to States, taking into account their institutional capacities, technical capabilities and varying administrative arrangements.
Highlighting the importance of efficient financial management, he stressed that funds allocated to the Department should be utilised effectively and speedily by the States.
Shri Dilip Kumar emphasised the importance of identifying a set of essential parameters to be followed uniformly by all States, while allowing flexibility in adopting other desirable parameters according to local requirements. He called for robust baseline data and comprehensive impact assessments to evaluate the outcomes of WDC-PMKSY 2.0, identify implementation gaps and draw lessons for the effective design and execution of WDC-PMKSY 3.0.
He further stressed that watershed development should remain focused on tangible outcomes for farmers and communities. Scientific interventions must translate into practical, location-specific solutions that can be effectively implemented at the grassroots level. He also called for recognising and motivating well-performing States and field-level officers to strengthen institutional commitment and improve implementation.
Shri Dilip Kumar observed that the proposed National Technical Guidelines should be finalised with a practical and implementable approach. He expressed confidence that achieving 80–90 per cent of the intended objectives through a flexible and realistic implementation framework would be more meaningful than adopting overly rigid standards.
Dr. C.S. Kumar, CEO, NRAA, highlighted the critical importance of data accessibility and availability for effective planning and implementation of watershed development programmes. He stressed the need for comprehensive capacity building of stakeholders at different levels and advocated effective utilisation of legacy datasets and existing scientific information. He also emphasised the development of a harmonised national-level Decision Support System, incorporating the best features of the systems developed by Odisha and Karnataka, to facilitate effective and integrated watershed planning.
Speaking on the occasion, Shri Nitin Khade highlighted the importance of finalising the National Technical Guidelines (NTGs) in a time-bound manner, stating that the consultation was an important step towards completing the draft guidelines. He emphasised that the guidelines would serve as a foundational framework  for future watershed development programmes.
Referring to India's vision of becoming a developed nation by 2047, Shri Khade highlighted the aspiration to contribute towards building a drought-resilient India through the scientific treatment of rainfed areas.
Emphasising the importance of Land Resource Inventory (LRI), he stated that LRI-based scientific data, digital soil libraries and Decision Support Systems (DSS) can transform watershed planning and implementation. These tools can enable village communities and individual farmers to make informed decisions regarding soil and water conservation plans, cropping patterns and nutrient management through accessible digital platforms.
He appreciated the contribution of ICAR-NBSS&LUP and the Soil and Land Use Survey of India (SLUSI) in developing digital soil mapping databases covering large areas. He emphasised that the extent of LRI coverage under future watershed development programs should be determined by considering the availability of existing datasets, implementation timelines, cost-effectiveness and field-level feasibility.
Shri Khade also highlighted the need to accelerate project implementation under WDC PMKSY 2.0. He noted that project timelines had progressively been reduced from seven years under WDC-PMKSY 1.0 to five years under WDC-PMKSY 2.0.
He further emphasised the need for appropriate use of GIS, remote sensing, high-resolution satellite imagery and drone technology, depending on local requirements.
Highlighting the importance of community participation, he stressed the need to strengthen Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs), User Groups ( UGs),Self-Help Groups (SHGs) and other community-based institutions for livelihood enhancement, value addition and better market access. He also underlined the need to strengthen community ownership and participation in the maintenance of water harvesting structures beyond the project period.
Dr. N.G. Patil, Director, ICAR-NBSS& highlighted the significance of Land Resource Inventory as a holistic, science-based approach for integrated watershed planning and landscape development.
The consultation is witnessing participation from representatives of the Department of Land Resources, NRAA, World Bank, REWARD project States of Odisha and Karnataka, NGOs, consortium partners including ICRISAT, WASSAN, NRSC and MANAGE, NABARD and various ICAR institutes.
The two-day consultation provides a platform for detailed technical deliberations and knowledge sharing on LRI, hydrological assessments, GIS and remote sensing applications, Decision Support Systems, community participation, livelihood interventions and monitoring and evaluation mechanisms.
The deliberations are expected to contribute towards finalising the National Technical Guidelines under the World Bank-assisted REWARD programme. These guidelines will also serve as an important technical input for WDC-PMKSY 3.0, facilitating science-based, cost-effective, scalable and participatory watershed planning, implementation and monitoring across States.
The consultation reaffirms the collective commitment of national and State-level institutions towards building climate-resilient landscapes, strengthening water security and improving the livelihoods of farming communities through scientific and sustainable watershed management.

title: Department of Rural Development and DAHD Join Hands to Boost Fodder Production, Strengthen Livestock Infrastructure and Support Rural Livelihoods under VB–G RAM G
subtitle:
Centre Issues Joint Advisory to States/UTs to Improve Fodder Availability and Promote Livestock Development in Rural Areas

22 Permissible Works Identified for Fodder Cultivation, Pasture Development, Dairy Infrastructure and Veterinary Facilities

Viksit Gram Panchayat Plans to Drive Fodder Security, Livestock Development and Sustainable Rural Livelihoods
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                05 NOV 2026 10:22AM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Department of Rural Development (DoRD), Ministry of Rural Development, and the Department of Animal Husbandry and Dairying (DAHD), Ministry of Fisheries, Animal Husbandry and Dairying, have jointly issued an advisory to all States and Union Territories to strengthen fodder security, pasture development and livestock-supportive infrastructure through convergence under the Viksit Bharat–Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin): VB–G RAM G Act, 2025.
The initiative adopts a whole-of-government approach to address fodder scarcity, strengthen livestock-related infrastructure and support the livelihoods of rural households, particularly small and marginal farmers and landless families dependent on livestock and dairy activities. It seeks to align rural employment and asset creation with the requirements of the livestock sector, while ensuring compliance with the provisions and planning framework of the Act.
The VB–G RAM G Act, which came into force on 1 July 2026, provides a statutory guarantee of 125 days of wage employment per rural household and focuses on the creation of durable assets across four thematic areas, including livelihood-related infrastructure and mitigation of extreme weather events. The joint advisory seeks to leverage this framework to promote fodder production, develop community pastures and strengthen livestock-supportive infrastructure.
22 Permissible Works Identified for Fodder and Livestock-Related Infrastructure
The advisory identifies 22 relevant works from the list of 375 permissible works under the VB–G RAM G framework. These cover interventions relating to fodder cultivation and storage, pasture development, livestock shelters, dairy infrastructure and veterinary health facilities.
Key interventions include:
Fodder cultivation for individual households and communities.
Development of community fodder resources, pastures, grazing lands and silvipasture.
Fodder storage facilities, fodder banks, silage units and other eligible fodder-related assets.
Construction, repair and maintenance of livestock shelters for eligible beneficiaries and communities, including cattle, goat, piggery and poultry shelters, as specified in the approved list.
Construction and repair of community milk collection centres.
Construction and repair of community veterinary health centres.
Construction of community cattle and animal troughs.
Construction of Azolla tanks for individual beneficiaries, as included in the approved list.
These interventions are intended to improve fodder availability, strengthen livestock-supportive infrastructure and contribute to more sustainable livestock-based livelihoods. All works will be undertaken in accordance with the approved list of permissible works and the applicable provisions of the Act, Rules and Guidelines.
Viksit Gram Panchayat Plans to Drive Local Priorities
The advisory emphasises decentralised, bottom-up and Panchayati Raj Institution (PRI)-led planning, with fodder development and livestock-supportive infrastructure integrated into Viksit Gram Panchayat Plans (VGPPs) and aligned with local development priorities approved through the Gram Sabha.
States and Union Territories are encouraged to endeavour to progressively increase expenditure on fodder and livestock-supportive works towards at least 5% of total programme expenditure, wherever supported by local needs, approved plans and applicable guidelines.
A need-based saturation approach is also encouraged to identify eligible households and communities requiring fodder and livestock-related assets. Gram Panchayats may give particular attention to areas with significant livestock dependence, including Gram Panchayats where more than 30% of the population is livestock-dependent, based on local requirements and priorities.
State-specific Fodder Resource Development Plans prepared by the ICAR–Indian Grassland and Fodder Research Institute (ICAR–IGFRI) may serve as guiding documents for planning at the district and block levels. The advisory also encourages attention to climate-resilient interventions, including suitable fodder varieties, perennial grasses and integrated crop–livestock systems, wherever relevant and covered under the permissible works.
Interdepartmental Convergence and Monitoring
The advisory calls upon States and Union Territories to prepare comprehensive State Action Plans for fodder security and livestock infrastructure through convergence among the Departments of Rural Development, Animal Husbandry, Agriculture and other relevant sectors.
The coordinated approach is intended to improve planning, facilitate effective use of available resources and ensure that investments respond to local requirements and support sustainable livestock-based livelihoods.
Strict Compliance with Statutory Safeguards
The advisory reiterates that all fodder development and livestock-supportive works must adhere to the applicable provisions of the VB–G RAM G Act, 2025. These include decentralised and PRI-led planning, compulsory social audit, the district-level ceiling of 40% on the material component, selection of individual beneficiaries in accordance with provisions under Schedule I, weekly public disclosure and grievance redressal.
States and Union Territories have also been urged to ensure that the approved advisory is disseminated among the concerned departments, Panchayati Raj Institutions and field functionaries to facilitate effective planning and implementation.
The advisory underscores the importance of coordinated action by State Governments and Union Territoriesto ensure that fodder security and livestock-supportive infrastructure receive due attention in rural development planning.
Strengthening Rural Livelihoods towards Viksit Bharat @2047
The joint advisory marks an important step towards integrating rural employment, natural resource management and livestock development. By linking permissible works under VB–G RAM G with local fodder and livestock infrastructure needs, the initiative seeks to improve fodder availability, support dairy and animal husbandry activities and strengthen livelihood opportunities for rural households.
Through convergence, decentralised planning and coordinated implementation, the initiative aims to help States and Panchayati Raj Institutions create durable assets that respond to local needs, support climate-resilient rural development and contribute to the broader vision of Viksit Bharat @2047.

title: Team led by Indian astronomers redefine star cluster UBC 63 as a double cluster system spotted after close flyby
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                05 NOV 2026 5:38PM by PIB Delhi
content:
UBC 63, a poorly populated
group of stars, bound loosely by gravity (Galactic open cluster) about 4892 light years away from the Earth, which was previously identified as a single star cluster, has now been found to be composed of two distinct star clusters.
The chance discovery provided a rare opportunity to study the aftermath of a close flyby between two stellar systems and offers new insights into the dynamical evolution of star clusters in the Milky Way.
Star clusters are important building blocks of galaxies. They are groups of stars that form within the same large reservoirs of gas and dust and subsequently evolve under the influence of their own gravity as well as the broader Galactic environment. Among them, historically, UBC 63 has remained largely overlooked, with limited literature providing only preliminary parameter estimates that presumed it to be a single cluster.
A team led by Astronomers from India, including a Department of Science and Technology (DST) INSPIRE Senior Research Fellow (SRF) and researchers of the Gauhati University, and researchers of the Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA), a DST autonomous institution, who set out to investigate star formation dynamics within the UBC 63 cluster using data from the European Space Agency's (ESA) Gaia mission discovered to their surprise that UBC 63 actually consists of two clusters, UBC 63A and UBC 63B, that recently passed remarkably close to each other.
Encounters between star clusters are relatively uncommon. Detecting a system soon after such an encounter can therefore provide valuable clues about how gravitational interactions influence cluster structure, motion and long-term evolution.
Gaia which provides exceptionally precise measurements of the positions and motions of stars across the Milky Way, showed that the two clusters belong to starkly different ages.
The researchers studied the brightness and colours of the member stars of UBC 63 and found that the stars formed two distinct sequences in the colour magnitude diagram, a key astronomical tool used to investigate the evolutionary stages of star clusters. This indicated that UBC 63 might actually consist of two separate stellar systems.
Fig
: Artist’s impression of two star undergoing a close encounter. (Credit: Gemini)
A detailed analysis of the stellar motions and other properties, using robust machine learning techniques and advanced dynamical simulations powered by high-performance computing, confirmed the presence of two distinct populations, now designated UBC 63A and UBC 63B. The two clusters have markedly different ages. UBC 63A is a young cluster, approximately 21 million years old, whereas UBC 63B is much older, with an estimated age of about 562 million years
.
This substantial age difference demonstrates that the two systems did not originate as a single cluster.
The researchers then investigated how two clusters with such different histories came to be located so close to each other. By simulating their motions through the Milky Way, the study found that, at the time when the younger cluster formed, the two systems were separated at about 60 parsecs (approx. 196 light years). The two clusters came remarkably close to one another about 6 million years ago, up to a separation of only about 7 parsecs (approx. 23 light years).
Today, the two clusters are approximately 26 parsecs (approx. 85 light years) apart. Their motion shows that they are not gravitationally bound to each other. Instead, they are moving apart after a close encounter.
The study demonstrates the power of modern astronomical surveys such as Gaia to uncover hidden structures that can remain unnoticed when stars are viewed only in projection on the sky.
The research published in Astronomical Journal was carried out by Samrat Biswas, an INSPIRE Senior Research Fellow (SRF) at Gauhati University; Biman J Medhi from Gauhati University; Sergio Messina (INAF – Catania Astrophysical Observatory); Zhanpeng Zhu (Shanghai Normal University); Songmei Qin (Shanghai Astronomical Observatory); Sukanta Deb (Cotton University); A. H. Sheikh (also an INSPIRE SRF at Gauhati University); H. S. Das (Assam University); Motohide Tamura (The University of Tokyo); Maheswar Gopinathan (Indian Institute of Astrophysics) and Ram Sagar (Indian Institute of Astrophysics).

title: Ministry of Textiles Successfully concludes Special Campaign 6, achieving significant milestones in Swachhata and Sustainability
date:

content:
The Ministry of Textiles successfully concluded Special Campaign 6, conducted from 2nd to 31st October 2026, with active participation from its attached and subordinate offices, autonomous bodies and Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs). The campaign focused on promoting cleanliness, improving administrative efficiency, reducing pendency, strengthening record management and encouraging sustainable waste disposal. Special Campaign 6 witnessed active participation from
all subordinate offices and organizations under the Ministry of Textiles.
These organizations undertook various activities, including
cleanliness drives, plantation programmes, scrap disposal, e-waste management, record management and other initiatives
, contributing significantly to the successful implementation of the campaign. Also to ensure effective planning, coordination and monitoring,
a dedicated committee was constituted under the chairmanship of the Deputy Director General (DDG), comprising three members
.
Under the campaign, the Ministry and its associated organizations generated ₹
10,15,814/- through scrap disposal
and
freed 44,025 square feet of office space
. Out of
20,950 physical files reviewed, 8080 were weeded out
, while
6,727 e-files were reviewed and 996 were closed.
Cleanliness activities were conducted
at 242 sites
. The Ministry also achieved
100% disposal of Public Grievances and Public Grievance Appeals
against the targets set. Further, implementation reports for
9 out of 26 Parliamentary Assurances were sent to the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs
.
Also in
E-waste management initiative, revenue of ₹3,62,096/-
has been realized so far. The remaining anticipated revenue is under recovery and will be credited in due course.
Important Activities Undertaken by the Ministry of Textiles under Special Campaign 6
Several initiatives were undertaken to promote environmental awareness and institutional cleanliness. The campaign commenced on 2nd October 2026 at NIFT Delhi with a tree plantation drive inaugurated by Secretary (Textiles), in the presence of senior officers.
Gandhi Jayanti Marked with Swachhta and Cleanliness Activities at NIFT Delhi
As
part of
Special Campaign 6,
the Ministry of Textiles organized a
Cyber Security Awareness Workshop
to sensitize officers and staff about the importance of
cyber security and safe digital practices.
The session focused on emerging
cyber threats, phishing and other online risks, password security, safe handling of digital information, and responsible use of official IT systems.
The initiative aimed to strengthen cyber hygiene, enhance awareness among employees, and promote a secure digital working environment across the Ministry and its subordinate organizations.
Under
Special Campaign 6,
the Ministry of Textiles placed special emphasis on
Effective management of e-waste through its identification, collection, segregation and systematic disposal.
Various offices and subordinate organizations were encouraged to undertake e-waste disposal as part of the campaign, ensuring that obsolete electronic items were handled in an environmentally responsible manner. Awareness activities, including a
session on e-waste management
,
quiz and essay competitions,
were also organized to promote understanding of the environmental impact of e-waste and encourage sustainable practices among officers and staff.
A dedicated textile waste collection initiative,
“Textiles for Tomorrow (पुरानेवस्त्र
,
नईसंभावनाएँ
)
”,
was undertaken in collaboration with the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs to promote reuse, recycling and sustainable management of textile waste.
The initiative has received an encouraging response,
with a total of 1003 kg
of post-consumer textile waste collected through the drive.
Craft from Waste’ – Promoting Creativity and Reuse
In an innovative initiative reflecting NIFT's creative and design-oriented ethos, the institute undertook the ‘Craft from Waste’ activity, demonstrating how discarded materials can be transformed into useful and decorative articles. These creatively prepared items were also used to beautify identified campus areas, promoting the principles of reuse, recycling and waste reduction.
Publicity and Outreach
The Ministry undertook extensive publicity through PIB releases and social media platforms to highlight the achievements of its subordinate organizations. A total of
12 PIB
releases and
2,960
social media posts were published, comprising
2,055
static creative posts and
690 reels/shorts
. The campaign achieved
2,80,697 reach/impressions
and
40,854 engagements
through likes, shares and comments.
The successful conclusion of Special Campaign 6 reflects the Ministry of Textiles continued commitment to Swachhata, sustainable resource management, transparency and efficient governance through coordinated efforts across its organizations

title: Bureau of Indian Standards Hallmarking
subtitle: The Mark Behind Consumer Trust
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                05 NOV 2026 2:07PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Hallmarking helps consumers make informed choices by providing
assurance about the purity of gold and silver jewellery.
The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) oversees this system through prescribed standards, digital traceability, and regulatory checks
.
Since
Mandatory gold hallmarking
was introduced in 2021,
over 65 crore gold articles
have received
Hallmark Unique Identification
(HUID) numbers as of 15 October 2026. The
number of BIS-registered jewellers
also
rose from 43,153 to 2,36,624
during the same period
.
For silver, while hallmarking remains voluntary, HUID-based marking became mandatory for all hallmarked silver articles on 1 September 2025, with
over 90 lakh silver items
hallmarked with HUID. Digital verification through the
BIS CARE App
and continued surveillance help consumers check jewellery details and support greater transparency in the market.
Gold and the Need for Consumer Confidence
For generations, gold has held a special place in Indian households
, serving as both a cherished possession and a store of value. Families often buy gold to keep themselves secured against inflation and meet urgent needs by pledging jewellery for loans. However, the purity of gold jewellery is not always easy to determine.
Gold is too soft to withstand wear, so it is alloyed with other metals to make jewellery. While this process is necessary, it can also create opportunities for adulteration and misrepresentation of purity. Moreover, determining the actual gold content becomes even more challenging in intricate jewellery with multiple joints or gold-plated articles. Recognising the need to protect consumers from
such practices,
the government took steps towards standardising gold products and
introducing hallmarking in the country.
What is Hallmarking?
Hallmarking is an important consumer protection measure that
certifies the purity of precious metal articles
against prescribed standards
.
It helps consumers make informed purchases and reduces the risk of paying for a higher purity than they receive.
The Hallmarking Scheme: From Voluntary to Wider Coverage
In order to address the regulatory vacuum in the Indian
gold market
, the
voluntary Hallmarking Scheme was launched in 2000.
The
Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS)
was identified as the sole agency to operate the Hallmarking Scheme in India.  BIS was entrusted with implementing the scheme to protect consumers against cheating. It was also tasked with developing export competitiveness and helping India emerge as a leading global market for gold jewellery.
The
Hallmarking Scheme for silver articles was launched in 2005
.  At present,
gold and silver
are covered under the Hallmarking Scheme in India.
For
gold jewellery
, hallmarking became
mandatory from 23 June 2021 in 256 districts
. With the expansion of Assaying and Hallmarking Centres, the
coverage has now expanded to
392 districts
. The hallmarking framework covers
7 gold caratages
(fineness in parts per thousand) under IS 1417:
9K (375), 14K (585), 18K (750), 20K (833), 22K (916), 23K (958), and 24KS (995)
.
While silver hallmarking remains
voluntary
, any silver article hallmarked under the BIS scheme must bear a
mandatory Hallmark Unique Identification (HUID) code
as of
1 September 2025
. Hallmark Unique Identification (HUID) is a
unique six-digit alphanumeric code
marked on each hallmarked jewellery article, making it traceable. Under the revised
IS 2112:2025
standard, silver jewellery and artefacts can be hallmarked in
eight grades of fineness
(in parts per thousand):
800 (800.0), 835 (835.0), 900 (900.0), 925 (925.0), 958 (958.0), 970 (970.0), 990 (990.0), and 999 (999.0)
.
How to Identify Hallmarked Jewellery
There are
three important signs to look for
when buying hallmarked jewellery or artefacts:
For Gold Jewellery/Artefacts:
BIS Standard Mark:
the mark displays the BIS logo.
Purity/Fineness Mark:
indicates the purity of the jewellery, for example,
22K916.
HUID (Hallmark Unique Identification) Code:
the unique six-digit identification number assigned to the jewellery.
For Silver Jewellery/Artefacts:
BIS Standard Mark
with the word ‘SILVER’
Purity/Fineness Mark –
indicates the purity, for example, 925
HUID (Hallmark Unique Identification) Code:
the unique six-digit identification number assigned to the article.
Together, these three marks provide greater assurance about the jewellery purchased, because true elegance comes with the assurance of purity.
Hallmarking in Practice: From Request to Verification
BIS has established a structured process for hallmarking, covering jeweller registration, purity assessment, digital identification and regulatory oversight.
1. Registration and Testing Centres
The hallmarking process begins when jewellers who wish to sell hallmarked jewellery register with BIS. Jewellers can apply online on the
National Single Window System (NSWS) portal
:
https://www.nsws.gov.in/
. The portal can be accessed directly or through the BIS portal:
https://www.manakonline.in
. Registration is granted instantly, free of charge, and remains valid for a lifetime.
Jewellers must then submit their jewellery to a BIS-recognised Assaying and Hallmarking Centre (AHC). AHCs are the testing centres where the jewellery is tested. AHCs receive recognition from BIS after verification of their infrastructure, testing facilities, and qualified personnel.
2. Initiating Hallmarking Requests through the Digital Portal
In order to submit jewellery for hallmarking, jewellers are encouraged to initiate requests through the portal and use its facility for sending jewellery to AHCs. Registered jewellers can log in to
www.manakonline.in
, select the Hallmarking option, and initiate a request. They enter details such as the jewellery category, quantity, weight, declared purity, and selected AHC before submitting the request.
Alternatively, AHC personnel can initiate requests on behalf of jewellers who submit jewellery without using the portal. This digital process establishes a record of each consignment and supports traceability throughout hallmarking.
3. Testing and HUID Generation
Once the jewellery reaches an Assaying and Hallmarking Centre (AHC), its weight and purity are assessed using the prescribed equipment and procedures.
The machinery and equipment used in the hallmarking process, including weighing balances, X-ray fluorescence (XRF) machines and laser marking machines, must support
direct data transfer to centralised software
. This enables relevant data generated during the process to be recorded electronically and reduces manual data entry.
API-based integration of XRF machines
was implemented with effect from 01 September 2024 to eliminate the possibility of manual entry
,
accompanied by integrated weighment systems that capture balance readings directly.
After testing
, the BIS server generates a
unique six-digit alphanumeric HUID code
for each jewellery article. The HUID, along with the BIS Standard Mark and the applicable purity mark, is then marked on the jewellery article.
AHCs must also capture photographs of the jewellery article and its hallmark, including the HUID. Under provisions deployed on
08 June 2026
, these photographs and weights are uploaded directly to Manak Online.
4. Digital Monitoring and Traceability
BIS provides a provision in the portal for
recording the dates and times of activities undertaken at AHCs.
These timestamps help in
real-time monitoring of operations
and assess the time taken from receipt to dispatch of hallmarked jewellery. They also support scrutiny of whether testing occurred before laser marking.
Further, digital initiatives such as
automatic weight capture and the Transfer HUID facility
strengthen end-to-end traceability in the hallmarking supply chain. The Transfer HUID facility
enables jewellers to digitally transfer the unique HUID
through the BIS platform whenever gold jewellery changes hands between jewellers or outlets.
Phase 1, implemented on
1 June 2026
, have provision to transfer HUID when moving gold between corporate jewellers or from any jeweller to a corporate entity, helping prevent duplicate or fraudulent hallmarking
.
5. Regulatory Oversight: Checks Beyond the Counter
Digital monitoring complements BIS's physical surveillance and regulatory checks. BIS periodically visits jewellery sales outlets and randomly samples hallmarked articles for testing against relevant Indian Standards. BIS also conducts periodic surveillance audits to verify whether AHCs continue meeting the prescribed requirements.
It carries out several enforcement activities, including raids, based on complaints/information received on misuse of hallmarks. These actions help in protecting consumers and strengthening trust in the hallmarking system. In 2025-26,
more than 30 enforcement activities
were conducted against jewellers for such violations.
6. Verify Before You Buy: The BIS CARE App
BIS enables consumers to independently verify hallmarked gold and silver jewellery digitally through the
BIS CARE App
. Consumers can verify a hallmarked article by
entering its unique Hallmark Unique Identification (HUID) number.
The app provides details such as the article’s purity, product type, jeweller, and assaying and hallmarking centre. Furthermore, following digital upgrades deployed on
08 June 2026
, the app provides access to
photographs of the article, its marked hallmark, and automatically recorded weight
, allowing buyers to compare the physical item against official records before completing a purchase. The BIS CARE App is available free of charge on Android and iOS and supports 12 languages.
Together, digital traceability, equipment integration and physical surveillance strengthen accountability across the hallmarking system.
Hallmarking at a Glance: Expanding Reach and Awareness
BIS has
expanded hallmarking coverage
through a growing network of registered jewellers and Assaying and Hallmarking Centres, alongside consumer awareness initiatives.
Since the implementation of mandatory gold hallmarking in 2021, over
65 crore gold articles
have been
hallmarked with HUID
as of 15 October 2026. During this period, BIS-registered operative jewellers increased from
43,153 to 2,36,624
, while recognised Assaying and Hallmarking Centres (AHCs) grew from
948 to 1,565
.
For silver, HUID-based marking was introduced on 01 September 2025 for articles submitted under the voluntary hallmarking scheme, leading to
over 90 lakh HUID-hallmarked silver articles
.
Consumer awareness remains an important part of this effort. From 01 April to 31 October 2026, BIS Regional and Branch Offices organised
1,582 consumer awareness programmes
throughout the country. These programmes included Awareness Programme on Standards under Compulsory Certification, Hallmarking, Gram Panchayat Sensitization programmes etc.
Towards Greater Trust and Transparency
Hallmarking connects the purity of precious metals with the confidence consumers need when making jewellery purchases. Over the years,
the system has expanded through wider coverage
,
technology, and stronger traceability.
Unique identification codes
help verify jewellery details, while physical surveillance and regulatory checks support accountability. Consumer awareness initiatives further help buyers recognise hallmarked articles and make informed choices. By bringing together technology, transparency and accountability, BIS continues to make trust an essential part of every hallmark.

title: CAPEX Support Scheme to Promote Critical Mineral Processing
subtitle: A ₹2,814-Crore Push for Lithium and Nickel Domestic Processing
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                05 NOV 2026 1:56PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The
CAPEX Support Scheme to Promote Critical Mineral Processing
has been recently approved with an outlay of ₹2,814 crore. The scheme will run from
FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31
. It offers a
30% capital subsidy
to set up two Lithium and two Nickel processing plants. Beneficiaries will be chosen through a competitive two-stage process, with support released against project milestones. The scheme is expected to anchor about
₹10,000 crore of investment
. It will reduce import dependence, strengthen supply chain resilience and support electric mobility, battery storage, electronics, defence and speciality steel.
Building India's Critical Mineral Processing Capabilities
Critical minerals are essential to economic development and national security. They contribute to clean energy technologies, high-tech electronics, transport, telecommunications and defence. Their availability is also vital to the global transition towards a low-carbon economy. Processing of these minerals remains geographically concentrated in a few countries. This exposes global supply chains to geopolitical disruptions, price volatility and potential supply restrictions. Consequently, countries identify minerals according to national priorities and take measures to secure their supply chains.
India has identified
24 critical minerals
, including lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite and rare earth elements. The country's commitment to achieving net-zero emissions by 2070 further underscores their importance. However, India's requirements for refined intermediates and high-purity materials of key minerals are met largely through imports. To strengthen India's capabilities in domestic processing and reduce external dependence, the
CAPEX Support Scheme to Promote Critical Mineral Processing
has been approved by the Union Cabinet on 04 November 2026.
CAPEX Support Scheme to Promote Critical Mineral Processing
The scheme provides targeted capital expenditure (CAPEX) support for establishing domestic critical mineral processing facilities. Its primary objectives are:
Promote domestic processing capacity:
Help set up high-purity Lithium and Nickel processing plants. Lithium plants will process ores and concentrates (excluding brines) into battery-grade products, while nickel plants will produce Class-1 nickel or battery-grade nickel sulphate, with cobalt recovery. CAPEX support will offset high upfront costs and improve project viability.
Build a resilient value chain:
Strengthen the Lithium and Nickel value chain by filling the missing link in processing.
Financial Outlay and Support
The scheme has a total outlay of
₹2,814 crore
. It will run for five years, from
FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31
. The scheme offers a
capital subsidy of 30%
of eligible investment for setting up
four processing plants
. These include two Lithium plants of at least
30 kt
capacity each and two Nickel plants of at least
50 kt
capacity each.
Support is capped at
₹500 crore
per Lithium beneficiary and
₹900 crore
per Nickel beneficiary. This amounts to ₹1,000 crore for Lithium and ₹1,800 crore for Nickel, totalling ₹2,800 crore. A further
₹14 crore
, or 0.5% of the outlay, is set aside for administrative expenses. The scheme will be fully funded through budgetary support from the Government of India.
Selection of Beneficiaries and Disbursement of Incentives
The scheme follows a competitive selection process. Support is then released in stages, linked to clear project milestones.
Two-Stage Selection Process
Stage 1 – Technical qualification:
All applications will be assessed on technical criteria. Only qualified applicants will move to the next stage.
Stage 2 – Financial bidding:
Qualified applicants will submit financial bids. Selection will follow the
least-cost criterion
, that is, the lowest CAPEX support sought.
Two beneficiaries
will be selected for each mineral, making four in total.
Milestone-Linked Disbursement
Incentives will be released in
three tranches
. Each tranche is linked to specific investment and equity milestones.
Tranche
Milestone
Cumulative Subsidy Released (% of Quoted Bid Amount)
